body: Atlas/browser review of implemented sidecar.scala — NEEDS-CHANGES, one type defect plus one browser seam. HIGH (lines 28-40,108-127,266-295): SidecarTrack.validated/Decoder choose Scalar vs Vector solely from runtime FeatureValueSchema and never bind that schema to V. Thus a scalar wire can decode as SidecarTrack[T,Vector[Double]] and materialize a vector-valued track whose FeatureSpace schema is Scalar; a Vector(1) wire can decode/materialize as SidecarTrack[T,Double] with a Vector schema. Add a closed numeric-value witness (or specialized checked factories/decoders) tying Double↔Scalar and Vector[Double]↔positive Vector(d), and pin both cross-typed decode/materialize rejections. MEDIUM/browser (177-212): header math is correct and portable—16-byte aligned offset, checked sizes, manual LE, no JVM-only ByteBuffer; JVM/JS/Native evidence supports that. But the only public read path takes Array[Byte] and decodeRows allocates Vector[Vector[Double]], so it is not the Atlas zero-copy resolver seam. Expose checked layout math (payloadOffset=16, valueCount, rowStride/rowByteOffset, dtype; safe Either, not SidecarManifest.expectedByteLength unchecked) so a Scala.js adapter can validate then use Float32Array/Float64Array on little-endian hosts and DataView fallback otherwise. Keep decodeRows as the portable materializer. Full-file checksum necessarily proves only a full fetch; per-tile sidecars/block receipts remain the later range-loading answer. LOW: docs call the header length uint64 while the reader deliberately accepts only signed-Long/Array capacity; state that supported subset. Aside from those: canonical compact rows, target/space/row validation, magic/version, raw-bit laws, finite scans, and privacy statement look sound.
